Oturum açıldı. Ama önce önemli bir ayrım: **Entire'ın kendi kaydı eksik.**

## Entire ne biliyor, ne bilmiyor

`entire session list` sadece 2 oturum gösteriyor: bu yeni oturum ve 11 Ağustos 16:54'teki **Entire kurulum oturumu** (checkpoint `01KZRVZ8V3GCEFGVQHVV9WP86W`, master'da).

Asıl çalıştığımız oturum — v2 correctness overhaul, 11 Ağustos 21:00 → 12 Ağustos 02:09 — Entire'da **yok**:

```
$ entire session info 0a834bd6-8056-4600-9d54-261e4d626977
Session not found.
```

`entire checkpoint list` de bu branch'te **0 checkpoint** diyor; tek checkpoint master'da duruyor. Yani hooks kurulu olmasına rağmen o oturum yakalanmamış. Bağlamı Claude'un yerel transkriptinden (`0a834bd6…jsonl`, 1186 satır) okudum.

## Nerede kalmıştık

**Branch:** `fix/v2-correctness-overhaul`, origin ile senkron, working tree temiz. 4 commit:

| Commit | İş |
|---|---|
| `c758a36` | fix!: dönüşüm çekirdeği — doğruluk + thread safety yeniden yazımı |
| `3168ce9` | build: analyzer zorunlu, SDK pinlendi, release hattı düzeltildi |
| `38b353e` | docs: README + CHANGELOG doğrulanmış çıktıya göre yeniden yazıldı |
| `2d63448` | test: bunların hepsini yakalayacak test paketi |

**PR #3 açık ve birleşmeye hazır** — https://github.com/keparlak/NumWordify/pull/3
`state: OPEN · mergeable: MERGEABLE · mergeState: CLEAN` — 7 check'in 7'si yeşil (ubuntu + windows build/test, CodeQL csharp + actions, Snyk, submit-nuget). Açık issue yok.

## Kaldığımız yerde duran üç seçenek

1. **Üçüncü thermos turu** — son turda eklenenler (`scaleKinds`, `AmbiguousCurrencyException`, `defaultCurrency`, deprecated locale çözümü, placeholder boşluk kuralı, snapshot altyapısı) bağımsız incelemeden geçmedi. Önceki iki tur da düzeltmenin kendisinde kusur bulmuştu — açık borç bu.
2. **Kural motoru (v3)** — iki incelemenin de asıl mimari önerisi; test güvenlik ağı artık hazır olduğu için ilk kez yapılabilir.
3. **Merge + v2.0.0 tag** — yayın hattı düzeltildi ama gerçek bir tag ile hiç denenmedi.

Küçük bir kalıntı: `actions/checkout@v4` ve `setup-dotnet@v4` Node 20 hedefliyor, deprecation uyarısı veriyor — v5 yükseltmesi ayrı bir iş.

İki şeyi teklif edeyim, ikisi de senin onayınla:
- Kayıp oturumu Entire'a bağlayayım mı (`entire session attach 0a834bd6-…`)? Bu, git ref'i yazar — o yüzden sormadan yapmadım.
- Hangi maddeden devam ediyoruz? Önerim **1** — merge etmeden önceki son doğrulama penceresi burası.

# Deep Code Quality Audit — `fix/v2-correctness-overhaul` (PR #3, NumWordify 2.0.0)

Verified locally: clean build under `TreatWarningsAsErrors`, **277 tests green** on net9.0 / net8.0 / net48.

## 0. The central question, answered with measurements

Two prior rounds asked for a rule engine. I measured the code before judging it.

`Converters/NumberToWordsConverter.cs` — 585 lines total:

| | lines |
|---|---|
| XML doc comments | 132 |
| blank | 91 |
| `//` comments | 20 |
| **actual code** | **342** |

Of those 342, roughly 90 are the nine constructors and their plumbing. **The conversion algorithm itself is about 200 lines.**

Per-method control flow (measured, `Converters/NumberToWordsConverter.cs`):

```
ConvertWholeNumber   L316  lines=51  branch-tokens=7  max nesting=4
Render               L258  lines=48  branch-tokens=4  max nesting=3
SplitNumberParts     L511  lines=32  branch-tokens=3  max nesting=2
ResolveCurrencyCode  L558  lines=26  branch-tokens=4  max nesting=4
ResolveCurrency      L227  lines=21  branch-tokens=5  max nesting=2
ConvertGroup         L378  lines=20  branch-tokens=3  max nesting=2
HundredsWord         L399  lines=16  branch-tokens=2  max nesting=2
TensAndOnesWord      L423  lines= 8  branch-tokens=0  max nesting=1
```

No method exceeds 51 lines. Maximum nesting depth anywhere in the file is 4, in one method. There is no cyclomatic hot spot.

More importantly — **`TensAndOnesWord` (L423–430) is already a rule engine**, and a better one than a JSON-driven engine would be:

```csharp
return DropOneBeforeThousand(remainder, groupValue, scale)
    ?? OverrideBeforeFollowingWord(remainder, scale, followedByNoun)
    ?? GeneralOverride(remainder)
    ?? Teen(remainder)
    ?? Regular(remainder);
```

Five named, single-purpose, individually-testable rules; explicit priority order; documented in the XML doc directly above; total cost 8 lines; fully type-checked. That is the entire value proposition of a rule engine, delivered without the engine.

**The prior reviews diagnosed the wrong problem.** The limitation in this library is not tangled branching. It is **schema expressiveness** — and a rule engine does not fix that. I proved this empirically rather than asserting it.

### Empirical test: can a new language be added without touching C#?

I built the best possible Russian localization expressible in the current schema (scratchpad only, no repo files touched) and ran it against the library:

```
value     actual                            required Russian
1         OK    ОДИН РУБЛЬ                  ОДИН РУБЛЬ
2         WRONG ДВА РУБЛЕЙ                  ДВА РУБЛЯ        (paucal "few")
5         OK    ПЯТЬ РУБЛЕЙ                 ПЯТЬ РУБЛЕЙ
21        WRONG ДВАДЦАТЬ ОДИН РУБЛЕЙ        ДВАДЦАТЬ ОДИН РУБЛЬ  (n%10==1)
111       OK    СТО ОДИННАДЦАТЬ РУБЛЕЙ      СТО ОДИННАДЦАТЬ РУБЛЕЙ
1000      WRONG ОДИН ТЫСЯЧА                 ОДНА ТЫСЯЧА      (feminine)
2000      WRONG ДВА ТЫСЯЧ                   ДВЕ ТЫСЯЧИ       (feminine + few)
5000      OK    ПЯТЬ ТЫСЯЧ                  ПЯТЬ ТЫСЯЧ
2000000   WRONG ДВА МИЛЛИОНОВ               ДВА МИЛЛИОНА     (few)
5000000   OK    ПЯТЬ МИЛЛИОНОВ              ПЯТЬ МИЛЛИОНОВ
```

**5 of 10 fail, and every failure traces to exactly two missing concepts:**

1. **Plural category.** `ScaleWord` (L368–376) hardcodes `group > 1`, and `Inflect` (L307–308) hardcodes `value == 1m`. Both are 2-way. Russian/Polish need 3 (`one`/`few`/`many`), Arabic needs 4 (with a dual). Selection depends on `n % 10` and `n % 100`.
2. **Gender agreement with the following scale word.** `SpecialNumbers.SpecialBeforeScale` is one flat `Dictionary<int,string>` applied before *any* scale of a given kind. Russian needs `ОДНА/ДВЕ` before `ТЫСЯЧА` but `ОДИН/ДВА` before `МИЛЛИОН` — i.e. keyed per scale index (or per grammatical gender), which the schema cannot express.

Neither is a branching problem. Both are **data-model extensions of maybe 40–60 lines** — and the first one *deletes* complexity: a proper `PluralCategory` selector subsumes `ScalesPlural`, `MajorSingular` and `MinorSingular` as special cases of one general mechanism.

A JSON rule engine would meanwhile destroy the single strongest asset in this PR: `LocalizationValidator.cs` (227 code lines) whose stated and delivered guarantee is *"a model that passes here can never fail later with a NullReferenceException or IndexOutOfRangeException from deep inside the conversion loop."* Predicates and actions expressed in JSON cannot be validated that way, cannot be type-checked, and cannot be unit-tested individually. That would be a strict regression.

**Credit where due:** `README.md` L209–215 ("Known limitations") already documents the French elision gap, Spanish gender, the dual/paucal gap, and German word-order inversion — accurately and without spin. This is unusually honest documentation and it materially de-risks the release.

---

## 1. Structural findings — should fix before tagging 2.0.0

These are all small, mechanical, and behavior-preserving. None requires the rule engine.

### 1.1 Two `[Obsolete]` properties scheduled for removal "in 3.0" — inside a 2.0 major release

`Models/SettingsModel.cs` L134–148: `UseCompoundNumbers` and `SkipOneForHundred`, both marked `[Obsolete("Has no effect... will be removed in 3.0")]`.

This is backwards. A major version is precisely the window in which removing them is free, and it is the window you are standing in right now. Deferring to 3.0 means the 2.0 public surface permanently ships two properties documented as doing nothing, plus two JSON keys silently ignored on load.

I verified deletion is completely free:
- **No shipped resource sets either key** (scanned all five `Resources/*.json`).
- `System.Text.Json` ignores unmapped members by default, so a 1.x JSON file that still carries them keeps loading.
- No test references either (grepped all 19 test files: `*** NONE ***`).

**Delete both.** −15 lines, −2 public API members, one fewer "why is this here" for every future reader.

### 1.2 `Currency` **and** `DefaultCurrency` — resolve the duality now

Yes, this is a design smell, and yes, it should be resolved before 2.0.0. The evidence is unusually clear-cut:

- **No shipped resource uses `currency`.** All five use `defaultCurrency` + `currencies` (I scanned every top-level key).
- `Models/LocalizationModel.cs` L14–17 — the property's own XML doc tells you not to use it: *"Prefer `DefaultCurrency`… naming it twice is how the two copies drift apart."* A model that documents one of its own fields as the wrong choice should not have that field.
- `LocalizationValidator.cs` L171–176 exists solely to police a mutual exclusion that a better type would make unrepresentable.
- `ResolveCurrency()` (L238–242) carries a two-branch ladder purely for this duality.
- The public convenience constructor `LocalizationModel(CurrencyModel, NumbersModel, SettingsModel?)` L78–83 sets the discouraged one.

**Recommendation:** delete `LocalizationModel.Currency`. Keep `Currencies` as the single storage and `DefaultCurrency` as the single selector. The convenience constructor writes into the map:

```csharp
public LocalizationModel(CurrencyModel currency, NumbersModel numbers, SettingsModel? settings = null)
{
    Currencies = new Dictionary<string, CurrencyModel> { ["DEFAULT"] = currency };
    DefaultCurrency = "DEFAULT";
    Numbers = numbers;
    Settings = settings ?? new SettingsModel();
}
```

Net: −1 public property, −10 validator lines, −1 branch in the hot path, and **one** way to name a default currency instead of two. Worth roughly 20 lines and, more importantly, one fewer invariant to police forever.

### 1.3 The 3×3 constructor matrix is implemented three times

This is the largest genuine duplication in the diff.

- `NumberToWordsConverter` has **9 constructors** = {`string culture`, `CultureInfo`, `LocalizationModel`} × {none, `CurrencyModel`, `string currencyCode`}.
- `DecimalExtensions` has **13 overloads** mirroring the same matrix.
- `DecimalExtensions.CreateConverter` (L145–169, 25 lines, 5 branches) **re-derives the same dispatch a third time**, and re-states precedence rules ("Localization over Culture", "Currency over CurrencyCode") that are already documented in `WordifyOptions`' XML docs.

`WordifyOptions` is *already* the canonical product type for this matrix. It just is not wired to the converter.

**Code judo:**

1. Add `public NumberToWordsConverter(WordifyOptions options)` as the single canonical resolution point.
2. Delete `CreateConverter` entirely; `ToWords(options)` becomes `new NumberToWordsConverter(options).Convert(number)`.

Net: **−25 lines of branching, one dispatch policy instead of three.** The precedence rules then live in exactly one place. (The ctor must read the options and retain nothing from it, to preserve the documented immutability.)

While you are there: 22 public entry points (9 ctors + 13 extensions) for a two-operation library is a lot of surface to support forever. 2.0 is the free window to trim it.

### 1.4 Six `null!` suppressions papering over a boundary the type system could express

`_localization.Numbers!` appears **6 times** (L312, 327, 370, 401, 472, 499), each preceded by a line like `var numbers = _localization.Numbers!;`.

The invariant is real: after `LocalizationValidator.Validate`, `Numbers` is never null. But the type still says `NumbersModel?`, so every consumer re-asserts it. This is exactly the "silent fallback papering over an unclear invariant" pattern — except here it's a suppression rather than a fallback, which is at least honest, just repetitive.

**Fix:** capture once in the constructors, where validation just ran.

```csharp
private readonly NumbersModel _numbers;
private readonly SettingsModel _settings;
// in each root ctor, after validation:
_numbers  = _localization.Numbers!;   // exactly one ! , at the boundary
_settings = _localization.Settings;
```

Every method then reads `_numbers` / `_settings` directly. Net: **−6 suppressions, −8 local-variable lines**, and the "validated" boundary becomes visible in the field declarations. This is consistent with the already-documented "must not be mutated after handover" contract, and does not defeat the `Pow10` guard (which reads a property, not a replaced object).

### 1.5 "What follows this group" is computed three different ways

This is the one place where the converter genuinely earns the "scattered special case" criticism, and it is cheap to fix.

The same concept is re-derived in three places with three different encodings:

- `ConvertWholeNumber` L341–342: `scaleIsNoun` / `followedByNoun`
- `HundredsWord` L407: `endsNumeralPhrase = scale == 0 || KindOf(scale) == ScaleKind.Noun`
- `OverrideBeforeFollowingWord` L446–447: `beforeNumeralAdjective` / `beforeNoun`

`KindOf(scale)` is called from three separate sites. On top of that, `ConvertWholeNumber` uses an `out bool endsWithNounScale` that one of its two call sites discards as `out _` (L277) — a classic sign the return type is wrong.

**Code judo:** compute the concept once, name it, thread it through.

```csharp
private enum Following { Nothing, NumeralAdjective, Noun }
```

At scale 0: `currencyFollows ? Following.Noun : Following.Nothing`. At scale > 0: `KindOf(scale) == ScaleKind.Noun ? Following.Noun : Following.NumeralAdjective`.

Then, provably equivalent:
- `HundredsWord`: `endsNumeralPhrase = following != Following.NumeralAdjective`
- `OverrideBeforeFollowingWord`: `beforeNumeralAdjective = following == Following.NumeralAdjective`; `beforeNoun = following == Following.Noun && ApocopateBeforeNoun`
- the out-param becomes `endsWithNounScale = scale > 0 && following == Following.Noun`

And change `ConvertWholeNumber` to return `(string Words, bool EndsWithNounScale)` so the `out _` disappears.

Net: three ad-hoc boolean derivations collapse into one named enum computed once, `KindOf` is called from one site instead of three, and the out-param goes away. This is the single highest-leverage readability change in the file.

---

## 2. Smaller findings

**2.1 Dead defensive branches in the `Render` replacer.** `NumberToWordsConverter.cs` L289–290: `currency is null ? string.Empty : Inflect(...)`. These arms are unreachable. `Render` is only called with `currency == null` for `NumberFormat`, and `LocalizationValidator.ValidateFormat` rejects `{major}`/`{minor}` in `numberFormat` (only `["whole","decimal"]` are allowed). The null check exists because the parameter type is `CurrencyModel?` while the real invariant is "currency is non-null iff the template mentions `{major}`/`{minor}`". Worth a comment at minimum; better, split `Render` so the invariant is structural.

**2.2 The placeholder whitespace rule is coherent but narrower than it looks.** `PlaceholderPattern` L31–33 with the captured leading space. Given §2.1, the *only* live case is a `CurrencyModel` with `Major = ""` or `Minor = ""` (legal — the validator rejects null but permits empty). `{whole}` and `{decimal}` can never be empty because both fall back to the validated-non-empty `ZeroWord`. So this is a correct addition, well-commented, serving one narrow real case. Minor gap: the regex captures at most one leading space, so a template with two spaces before a placeholder would leave a stray internal space that `.Trim()` cannot reach. Templates are author-controlled, so this is a note, not a bug.

**2.3 `AmbiguousCurrencyException` / `defaultCurrency` design — coherent, endorsed.** `AmbiguousCurrencyException` is a genuinely good addition: refusing to print "EUROS" for an `es-MX` amount is exactly the class of silent wrongness this PR exists to eliminate, and the error message names the fix. Deferring the throw to `Convert()` rather than the constructor is correct, because `ConvertWithoutCurrency("es-MX")` must keep working. `ScaleKind` is likewise a real grammatical concept (not a per-language flag), earns its place in both French and Spanish, and defaults sanely. These are coherent model additions, not bolt-ons.

Minor: `ResolveCurrency()` re-runs a 4-branch resolution on every `Convert()` call even though the converter is immutable and the answer is fixed at construction. Cosmetic given the cost, but it does mean the exception's *cause* (constructor arguments) is reported at a *distant* site.

**2.4 README states a workaround that does not exist.** `README.md` L213: *"Currency names distinguish only 'one' from 'not one'. Languages with dual or paucal forms need a custom localization."* A custom `LocalizationModel` **cannot** fix this — `Inflect` (L307) is hardcoded C# and `CurrencyModel` has exactly two slots. My Russian probe confirms it. The limitation statement is right; the offered escape hatch is not. Either drop the second sentence or say plainly that these languages are not supported.

**2.5 French `d'euros`.** 14 lines of `fr-FR.approved.txt` contain "UN MILLION EUROS" / "DEUX CENTS MILLIONS EUROS", which is not correct French. `README.md` L211 documents this honestly, and the reasoning (elision depends on the following word; `NounScaleLinkWord` is a fixed string, and fr-FR defines EUR/USD/CHF which elide differently) is sound. I am **not** calling this a blocker given the documentation — but note it is the same missing concept as §0: a context-sensitive form selector. When you add the plural-category mechanism, French elision falls out of it for free.

**2.6 CI does not test net6.0 or net7.0.** `ci.yml` installs all four SDKs and builds all five target frameworks, but the test project targets net9.0/net8.0/net48. The net48 leg does exercise the `netstandard2.0` build, which is the important one. Still, two shipped TFMs are compiled but never run. One line in the test csproj.

---

## 3. Test suite assessment

**Verdict: healthy, and the strongest part of this PR.** 277 tests, 1748 lines, organized coherently by concern (locale, feature, cross-cutting). `ThreadSafetyTests` with 20,000 parallel iterations against a shared converter is exactly the right test for the bug it guards. `ReadmeSchemaTests` — parsing the JSON block *out of README.md itself* and running it through the full validator — is genuinely excellent; it catches a misspelled key in documentation, which almost no library tests for.

**The golden snapshot approach pulls its weight.** 4 × 1058 lines, covering 0–1000 plus a magnitude ladder plus fractions, per locale. This is the right tool: it is what catches the "the hand-written table stopped at two million" class of bug, and a regression surfaces as a reviewable diff rather than silence. `AssertSameLines` reporting the first mismatching line (rather than a 40KB string diff) is a thoughtful touch. The `NUMWORDIFY_APPROVE=1` re-approval flow is standard and correctly documented. Maintenance drag is low because the inputs are a fixed list, not generated.

**One real gap.** The four newest grammar settings have **no test that exercises them in isolation**:

```
scaleKinds                   *** NONE ***
NounScaleLinkWord            *** NONE ***
ApocopateBeforeNoun          *** NONE ***
UseExactHundredsBeforeScale  *** NONE ***
```

They are covered only *indirectly*, through the two shipped locales that happen to set them — and always in the same combination. `TestLocalizations.cs` is a fixed English builder that cannot toggle any of them. These four settings interact combinatorially (see §1.5), so the untested combinations are precisely the ones a fifth language will hit first. Add a synthetic-locale theory that toggles each flag independently and asserts the documented behavior. This matters more than any refactor in §1.

**Acceptable duplication.** 88–96% of the hand-written per-locale `InlineData` cases are already covered by the golden snapshots (English 20/22, French 45/47, Spanish 28/30, Turkish 30/34). Normally I would push back on ~130 duplicated assertions — but here the hand-written tables carry the *intent* (each has an explanatory name and comment), while the snapshot carries the *coverage*. That is a defensible split. Leave it.

---

## 4. API surface, docs, exceptions

**Exception hierarchy: well designed.** A single `NumWordifyException` base with four sealed leaves, each carrying structured data alongside the message (`LocalizationNotFoundException.AvailableCultures`, `NumberOutOfRangeException.MaximumScaleCount`, `AmbiguousCurrencyException.RequestedCulture`/`ResolvedCulture`). Messages state the problem *and* the fix. `Exceptions/NumWordifyException.cs` at 136 lines for 5 types is appropriately compact — I would not split it.

One inconsistency: currency-code lookup failure throws `ArgumentException` (`NumberToWordsConverter.cs` L579) while every other library-level failure throws a `NumWordifyException` subtype. Arguable either way — it *is* a bad argument — but a caller writing `catch (NumWordifyException)` will miss it. Worth a deliberate decision, documented.

**XML docs: excellent, and unusually so.** 655 doc lines across the library. Critically, they explain *why*, with concrete examples (`"UN MILLÓN DE EUROS", but "UN MILLÓN QUINIENTOS MIL EUROS"` on `NounScaleLinkWord`; the French adjective/noun split on `ScaleKind`). The inline comments are the same quality — L232–234, L271, L388, L406–407, L444–445, L537 each explain a decision that would otherwise look arbitrary. This is a real asset and should not be trimmed.

**File sizes: all fine.** Largest library file is 585 lines (342 code). Nothing approaches 1k. Applying §1 would bring the converter to roughly 500 lines.

**Build/release infrastructure: solid.** `Directory.Build.props` with pinned `AnalysisLevel` and `TreatWarningsAsErrors` (with the reasoning for pinning spelled out); `publish.yml` deriving the version from the tag, rejecting SemVer build metadata that NuGet would strip, verifying the produced filename, and deliberately omitting `--skip-duplicate`. The `environment: nuget` gate is the right call. No findings.

---

## VERDICT: **SHIP 2.0.0 AS IS**

Not a rubber stamp — ship *after* the §1 cleanups, which total roughly 60 lines of deletion and half a day of work, plus the §3 test gap:

| | |
|---|---|
| 1.1 | Delete the two `[Obsolete]` settings properties (free, verified) |
| 1.2 | Collapse `Currency` + `DefaultCurrency` into one representation |
| 1.3 | Add `NumberToWordsConverter(WordifyOptions)`; delete `CreateConverter` |
| 1.4 | Cache `_numbers` / `_settings`; delete 6 `null!` suppressions |
| 1.5 | Replace three ad-hoc "what follows" booleans with one `Following` enum |
| 3 | Add a synthetic-locale test that toggles the four grammar flags in isolation |

1.1 through 1.3 are breaking changes and this is the last free window for them. 1.4 and 1.5 are pure internal cleanup and could follow.

**Do not build the rule engine.** The measured code does not justify it (200 lines of algorithm, max nesting 4, no method over 51 lines), the rule-chain pattern the reviewers wanted already exists in `TensAndOnesWord`, the real gap is schema expressiveness which a rule engine would not close, and a JSON-driven engine would destroy the validator's "cannot fail later" guarantee — the single best thing about this PR. When language five needs it, add a **plural-category selector** and **per-scale override maps**: two data-model extensions of roughly 60 lines that *delete* `ScalesPlural`, `MajorSingular` and `MinorSingular` as special cases, and hand you French elision for free.

### The strongest argument against my own verdict

The live behavior-flag count went from 3 to 7 while shipped languages went from 2 to 4 — and **two of the four new flags exist to serve exactly one language each** (`UseExactHundredsBeforeScale` is set only by fr-FR; `NounScaleLinkWord` only by es-ES). If that ratio holds, language eight arrives with roughly 15 boolean flags whose pairwise interactions nobody has tested — and today **not one of those four flags has a test that exercises it in isolation** (§3). That is precisely the failure mode of a flag-per-quirk architecture, and the earlier reviewers were pattern-matching on a real trend even though their diagnosis of the *current* state was wrong.

My counter is that these flags are named after grammatical concepts, not languages, and will be reused across families — Italian, Portuguese and Catalan will all want `ApocopateBeforeNoun`. But that is a prediction, not a measurement. **The way to test it is to add language five before 2.1 and count how many new flags it costs.** If the answer is two or more, the architecture question is genuinely open again, and I would want it settled before the flag count reaches double digits. Fix the §3 test gap now so that experiment is cheap to run.</result>

## CONFIRMED — High

### 1. The README's documented `CurrentCulture` guard does not work; `IsCultureSupported` is a misleading guard; the test asserting it is vacuous

- `README.md` §"Checking a culture before using it" (~line 113)
- `Converters/NumberToWordsConverter.cs:57,64` (`IsCultureSupported`), `:235-236` (throw site)
- `tests/NumWordify.Tests/ReadmeExampleTests.cs:90-98`

The README presents this as *the* safe way to use the machine culture:

```csharp
var culture = NumberToWordsConverter.IsCultureSupported(CultureInfo.CurrentCulture)
    ? CultureInfo.CurrentCulture.Name : "en-US";
amount.ToWords(culture);
```

`IsCultureSupported` answers "does a localization resolve?", but `Convert` additionally requires `RegionMatches`. The two questions differ for every culture that resolves by language fallback, so the guard passes and the very next line throws.

Reproduced (probe against `bin/Release/net9.0/NumWordify.dll`), running the recipe verbatim per machine culture:

```
machine=en-US  guarded->en-US  OK
machine=en-GB  guarded->en-GB  THROWS AmbiguousCurrencyException
machine=en-CA/AU/IN/NZ/IE/ZA   THROWS AmbiguousCurrencyException
machine=es-MX/AR/CO/CL         THROWS AmbiguousCurrencyException
machine=fr-CA/BE/CH            THROWS AmbiguousCurrencyException
machine=tr-CY                  THROWS AmbiguousCurrencyException
machine=de-DE  guarded->en-US  OK   (unsupported -> correctly falls back)
```

Enumerating every installed .NET culture: **`IsCultureSupported` returns `true` for 187 cultures; `ToWords` throws for 178 of them.** Only the 4 shipped specifics, the 4 neutrals, and `tr-TR-EUR` actually work.

`ReadmeExampleTests.Culture_fallback_example` runs that exact snippet but only asserts `Assert.False(string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(...))` on whatever the **ambient** culture produces. Nothing in the repo pins `CurrentCulture` (grep confirms line 93 is the only occurrence in tests, and no `DOTNET_SYSTEM_GLOBALIZATION*` env var in the workflows). On `ubuntu-latest` the culture is invariant → falls to `en-US`; on `windows-latest` it is `en-US`; on the maintainer's machine it is `tr-TR`. The test can never fail in any environment this project runs in, which is why a broken recipe shipped with a green suite.

The throw itself is intentional and well documented — I am **not** reporting that. What the author appears unaware of is that (a) the recommended workaround is broken, (b) there is no public API that answers "will `Convert` succeed?", and (c) `README.md` §Basic usage says *"`"EN-US"`, `"en"` and `"en-GB"` all resolve to `en-US`"* immediately under `ToWords` examples, which reads as if `1234.56M.ToWords("en-GB")` works. It throws.

Suggested fixes: make the test culture-parameterised over `en-GB`/`es-MX` (it will fail today), change the README recipe to `ToWordsWithoutCurrency` or an explicit currency code, and consider an API such as `IsCultureSupported(culture, out bool currencyApplies)` or `TryGetDefaultCurrency`.

## CONFIRMED — Low / Medium (developer experience)

### 2. `global.json` hard-pins the .NET 9 SDK band; .NET 9 is out of support as of May 2026
`global.json:1-6` — `"version": "9.0.100", "rollForward": "latestFeature"`. I verified empirically that `latestFeature` never crosses major.minor: a scratch `global.json` asking for `8.0.100/latestFeature` resolved to `8.0.424` (**not** the installed 9.0.314), and `11.0.100/latestFeature` fails with `A compatible .NET SDK was not found`. A contributor with only the .NET 10 SDK installed therefore cannot run `dotnet build`/`dotnet restore` at all. There was no `global.json` on `master`, so this is new. The README's Contributing section does not mention it. Note the stated justification ("a new SDK band cannot turn a release build red") is already served by `AnalysisLevel 9.0` in `Directory.Build.props`; `rollForward: latestMinor` would keep the analyzer pin while unblocking newer SDKs.

### 3. Test project targets `net48` on Windows with no reference-assembly package
`tests/NumWordify.Tests/NumWordify.Tests.csproj:8` adds `net48` on Windows, but there is no `PackageReference` to `Microsoft.NETFramework.ReferenceAssemblies`. It builds here and on `windows-latest` only because the 4.x targeting packs are machine-installed (VS / Build Tools). A Windows contributor with only the .NET SDK will hit `MSB3644: The reference assemblies for .NET Framework v4.8 were not found`. One `PackageReference` fixes it.

### 4. The process-wide cached culture array is handed out mutably
`Converters/LocalizationLoader.cs:68-78`, `NumberToWordsConverter.cs:44`, `Exceptions/NumWordifyException.cs` (`LocalizationNotFoundException.AvailableCultures`). Reproduced:

```
runtime type of SupportedCultures: System.String[]
before: en-US, es-ES, fr-FR, tr-TR
after mutating through a cast: PWNED, es-ES, fr-FR, tr-TR
exception message now: ... Available cultures: PWNED, es-ES, fr-FR, tr-TR.
ex.AvailableCultures same instance as SupportedCultures: True
```

`IReadOnlyList<string>` over a `string[]` is castable and mutable, and the corruption is permanent for the process. Not a trust-boundary crossing, but it contradicts the loader's own doc comment ("The cached instances are never handed out to callers, which is what makes sharing them safe"). Wrap in `ReadOnlyCollection<string>` or hand out a copy.

### 5. Validator does not cross-check `decimalPlaces` against `scales.Length`
`Converters/LocalizationValidator.cs:58-62` vs `NumberToWordsConverter.cs:277,338`. The fraction is rendered through `ConvertWholeNumber`, so `decimalPlaces > 3` needs a thousands scale word. A locale with `scales: [""]` and `decimalPlaces: 6` passes validation, then `Convert(1.123456m)` throws at runtime with a message that blames the wrong thing:

```
NumberOutOfRangeException: The number 1,123456 is too large for this locale:
it defines 1 scale word(s), so the largest convertible value is 10^3 - 1.
```

The whole part is `1`. Also note `1,123456` — `NumberOutOfRangeException`'s interpolated `{value}` uses `CurrentCulture` (`Exceptions/NumWordifyException.cs`); every other number→string in the output path correctly uses `InvariantCulture`. No shipped locale is affected; this only bites custom localizations.

### 6. Latent: a mixed-case resource filename would break `SupportedCultures`
`Converters/LocalizationLoader.cs:58-63,117-121`. `ResourceNames` filters with `EndsWith(".json", OrdinalIgnoreCase)`, but `Load` rebuilds the key as `CultureNameOf(name) + ".json"` (lowercase, ordinal) and `GetManifestResourceStream` is case-sensitive. A future `Resources/de-DE.JSON` would make `SupportedCultures` throw `InvalidLocalizationException` for every caller. All five shipped files are lowercase, so this is latent only.

367	## Migrating from 1.x
368	
369	Version 2.0 changes output for four of the five shipped locales, because that output was wrong. Re-check any golden files or stored strings.
370	
371	- **The ones digit is no longer dropped.** `1234.56M.ToWords("tr-TR")` was "BİN İKİ YÜZ OTUZ TL ELLİ Kr" and is now "BİN İKİ YÜZ OTUZ DÖRT TL ELLİ ALTI Kr". The same fix applies to `fr-FR` and `es-ES`.
372	- **Round hundreds no longer gain a trailing "ZERO"** in `en-US`: `100M` was "ONE HUNDRED ZERO USD ZERO Cents", now "ONE HUNDRED DOLLARS ZERO CENTS".
373	- **`en-US` currency names** changed from `USD`/`Cents` to `DOLLARS`/`CENTS`, with singular forms.
374	- **French and Spanish** are now grammatically correct for 0–99, for the `cent`/`ciento` forms and for scale agreement; almost every value in those languages changes.
375	- **Rounding** is away from zero rather than to even, so some values gain a minor unit.

20	  The ones digit is now always written; `specialNumbers.compoundSeparator` controls the
21	  separator, which is all the flag was ever meant to do.
22	- **`en-US` appended a stray "ZERO" to every value ending in two zeros.** A `"0": "ZERO"`
23	  entry in the special-numbers map was matched against the last two digits of each group,
24	  so `100` read "ONE HUNDRED ZERO USD ZERO Cents". A group whose last two digits are zero
25	  now contributes no tens/ones word at all, and the entry has been removed.
26	- **The converter was not thread safe.** The current scale lived in an instance field, so
27	  a shared instance produced wrong words and spurious "number is too large" failures under
28	  concurrency. Scale is now a local, making instances genuinely immutable.
29	- **Money rounded to even instead of away from zero**, turning `1.005` into one dollar and
30	  zero cents.
31	- **A value that rounded to zero kept its sign**: `-0.001` read "NEGATIVE ZERO ...".
32	- **A currency name containing a placeholder corrupted the output.** Templates were
33	  expanded with a chain of `string.Replace` calls, so a `Major` of `"{minor}"` was
34	  substituted twice. Expansion is now a single pass, and a placeholder that resolves to
35	  an empty string no longer leaves a double space.
36	- **`settings.skipOneForHundred` never did anything** — both branches of its condition
37	  produced the same word.
38	- **Supplying an incomplete `LocalizationModel` threw `NullReferenceException`** from
39	  inside the validator, and a `teens` array shorter than nine entries threw
40	  `IndexOutOfRangeException` mid-conversion. Both are now reported at construction time
41	  with a message naming the field.
42	- The original `JsonException` is now preserved as `InnerException` instead of being
43	  flattened into a string.
44	- **French dropped the plural of `cent` and `vingt` in front of `million` and `milliard`**,
45	  producing "DEUX CENT MILLIONS" where French requires "DEUX CENTS MILLIONS". The plural
46	  drops only before another numeral adjective, and `mille` is one while `million` is a
47	  noun — a distinction the locale now states through `numbers.scaleKinds`.
48	- **Spanish omitted the obligatory `de`** after a noun scale word: "UN MILLÓN EUROS"
49	  rather than "UN MILLÓN DE EUROS". Expressed through `settings.nounScaleLinkWord`, and
50	  correctly absent when the number ends in `MIL`.
51	- **A culture that resolved through language fallback borrowed the locale's default
52	  currency.** `ToWords("es-MX")` printed euros. It now throws
53	  `AmbiguousCurrencyException`; `ConvertWithoutCurrency` and an explicit currency both
54	  still work.
55	- **`WordifyOptions` silently ignored `CurrencyCode`** when `Localization` was also set,
56	  making the same mistake an error on one path and invisible on the other.
57	- A `null` entry in `scalesPlural` passed validation and threw `NullReferenceException`
58	  mid-conversion — and only for groups greater than one, so it hid at 1000 and appeared
59	  at 2000. An empty entry now means "fall back"; `null` is rejected.
60	- An empty entry in `scales` passed validation and silently dropped the scale word, so
61	  2000 and 2 produced the same words.
62	- A `CurrencyModel` passed to a constructor was never validated, so a `null` major unit
63	  rendered as an empty string instead of failing.
64	- `decimalPlaces: 0` combined with a `{decimal}` or `{minor}` placeholder appended the
65	  zero word to every amount. The combination is now rejected.
66	- A misspelled placeholder such as `{hole}` was printed literally. Format strings are now
67	  validated against the placeholders they support.
68	- `exactHundreds` required all ten entries, forcing Spanish to copy eight values out of
69	  `hundreds` and keep them in sync by hand. Empty entries now fall back.
70	- The blanket whitespace collapse that cleaned up after empty placeholders also rewrote
71	  separators a locale had chosen on purpose. An empty placeholder now takes its own
72	  preceding space with it instead.
73	
74	### Added
75	
76	- Test suite (`tests/NumWordify.Tests`): golden output tables per locale, concurrency
77	  tests, validation tests and range tests. Every README example is asserted, including
78	  the JSON schema block, which is parsed out of README.md rather than restated in C#.
79	- Full-output snapshots in `tests/NumWordify.Tests/Approvals`: every value from 0 to 1000
80	  plus a magnitude ladder, with and without currency, per locale. The hand-written tables
81	  stopped at two million, which is exactly where the French pluralisation bug lived.
82	  Re-approve with `NUMWORDIFY_APPROVE=1` and read the diff.
83	- CI workflow running build and tests on Linux and Windows for every push and pull
84	  request. Previously nothing was compiled before a release tag.
85	- `INumberToWordsConverter`, so consumers can substitute the converter in their own tests.
86	- `NumberToWordsConverter.SupportedCultures` and `IsCultureSupported`, so a culture can be
87	  probed without catching an exception.
88	- Localization caching. Each locale is parsed and validated once per process rather than
89	  on every call; `ToWords` was doing a full manifest scan and JSON parse per invocation.
90	- Per-locale currency maps and `ToWords(culture, "EUR")`, so one locale file can serve
91	  several currencies.
92	- Singular currency forms (`majorSingular`, `minorSingular`): `1.01` now reads
93	  "ONE DOLLAR ONE CENT".
94	- `settings.decimalPlaces` (0–6) for currencies without a minor unit or with three.
95	- `settings.decimalReading` to read the fraction digit by digit.
96	- `numbers.exactHundreds`, `numbers.scalesPlural`, `numbers.scaleKinds`,
97	  `specialNumbers.specialBeforeScale`, `settings.useExactHundredsBeforeScale`,
98	  `settings.apocopateBeforeNoun` and `settings.nounScaleLinkWord` — the rules French and
99	  Spanish need and a flat digit table cannot express.
100	- `LocalizationModel.DefaultCurrency`, so a locale names its default currency by key

100	- `LocalizationModel.DefaultCurrency`, so a locale names its default currency by key
101	  instead of spelling it out a second time next to the `currencies` map.
102	- `LocalizationModel.Deprecated`, which keeps a redundant locale resolvable by name while
103	  removing it from `SupportedCultures` and from language fallback.
104	- `global.json` and a pinned `AnalysisLevel`, so a new SDK band cannot turn a release
105	  build red without a code change.
106	- `WordifyOptions`, covering the combinations the overload matrix does not.
107	- Exception hierarchy rooted at `NumWordifyException`.
108	- Analyzers, `.editorconfig` and `TreatWarningsAsErrors` across the build.
109	
110	### Changed
111	
112	- **French is now grammatically correct** for 21, 31–61, 70–99 (`SOIXANTE ET ONZE`,
113	  `QUATRE-VINGTS`, `QUATRE-VINGT-ONZE`), for the plural of `cent` and `vingt`
114	  (`DEUX CENTS` but `DEUX CENT CINQUANTE`), for `MILLE` rather than `UN MILLE`, and for
115	  plural scale words (`DEUX MILLIONS`). Previously every value from 11 to 19 read as
116	  "DIX".
117	- **Spanish is now grammatically correct** for 11–19, the fused twenties
118	  (`VEINTIUNO`…`VEINTINUEVE`), `CIEN` versus `CIENTO`, the `Y` separator, apocope before
119	  scale words and currency names (`UN MILLÓN`, `VEINTIÚN EUROS`, `UN EURO`), and plural
120	  scale words. Previously every value from 11 to 19 read as "DIEZ".
121	- `en-US` currency names are now `DOLLARS`/`CENTS` with singular forms, matching what the
122	  documentation always claimed, instead of `USD`/`Cents`.
123	- Culture lookup is case-insensitive and falls back within a language, so `"EN-US"`,
124	  `"en"` and `"en-GB"` all resolve to `en-US`.
125	- `NumberToWordsConverter` is `sealed`.
126	- `LocalizationModel.Currency` and `.Numbers` are nullable, reflecting what was already
127	  true at runtime.
128	- `settings.useTeens` is `bool?`; unset means "use teens when they are supplied".
129	- The package version comes from the release tag. It was hardcoded to `1.0.0`, so every
130	  tag produced the same package and `--skip-duplicate` swallowed the push while the job
131	  reported success. `--skip-duplicate` has been removed.
132	- `System.Text.Json` is referenced only for the `netstandard2.0` target; the other targets
133	  have it in the box.
134	- `favicon.ico` is no longer packed into consuming projects, and the package icon dropped
135	  from 640 KB to 29 KB.
136	- Spanish now defines five scale words rather than six. The previous sixth, `BILLARDO`
137	  for 10^15, is not a word the RAE recognises; the convertible range stops at 10^15 − 1
138	  instead of inventing one. The other locales still reach 10^18 − 1.
139	- Documentation is now in English throughout, the .NET requirement is stated correctly
140	  (.NET 6.0+ or .NET Standard 2.0, not ".NET 9.0 or higher"), and the README carries a
141	  Known limitations section naming what the model still cannot express — French `d'`
142	  elision before a currency name, Spanish gender agreement, dual and paucal currency
143	  forms, and inverted word order such as German "einundzwanzig".
144	
145	### Deprecated
146	
147	- `settings.useCompoundNumbers` and `settings.skipOneForHundred` have no effect and will
148	  be removed in 3.0. They remain as `[Obsolete]` properties so existing code compiles.
149	- `tr-TR-EUR` is marked deprecated: excluded from `SupportedCultures` and from language
150	  fallback, resolvable only by exact name. Use `ToWords("tr-TR", "EUR")`, which a test
151	  proves produces identical output.
152	
153	### Removed
154	
155	- `FileNotFoundException` is no longer thrown for an unknown culture; catch
156	  `LocalizationNotFoundException` (or `NumWordifyException`) instead.
157	- The undocumented claim of caching support is gone from the README — replaced by actual
158	  caching.

  as `[Obsolete]` properties would have kept two do-nothing members in the public surface

  mutual-exclusion rule left to police. The single-currency constructor is unchanged.

  `LocalizationNotFoundException` (or `NumWordifyException`) instead.

Hepsi tamam. Sonuç:

## Kod — 5 madde, tek commit

`c675538 fix!: repair the culture guard and collapse the currency duality` — 13 dosya, +297/−127.

**1. Kültür koruması.** `IsCultureSupported(culture, out bool currencyApplies)` eklendi; `Convert`'ün gerçekten sorduğu soruyu cevaplıyor. README tarifi buna göre yeniden yazıldı, ve `en-GB`'nin neden `AmbiguousCurrencyException` fırlattığı üç satırlık örnekle gösterildi.

**2. README testi artık kırılabiliyor.** Makine kültürü üzerinden parametrize edildi — `en-US`/`en-GB`/`es-MX`/`es`/`de-DE`, her biri beklenen `supported` + `currencyApplies` çiftiyle. Eski tarife karşı çalıştırılsa kırmızı yanar. Ayrıca yeni `Culture_without_a_matching_region_examples` testi README'deki üç satırı doğruluyor.

**3. Dört dilbilgisi bayrağı tek tek test edildi.** Yeni `GrammarSettingsTests.cs` (10 test) + `TestLocalizations.GrammarProbe(scaleKinds)`. Sentetik locale kasten gerçek dile benzemiyor — `ExactHundreds[2] = "TWO HUNDREDS"` gibi görünür farklarla, ki bir bayrak çalışmayı bıraktığında sonuç aynı string olarak gizlenmesin. Her bayrağın açık/kapalı hali ayrı `InlineData`; ScaleKinds × ApocopateBeforeNoun etkileşimi de kapsandı. Hepsi ilk çalıştırmada geçti — yani bayraklar dokümante edildiği gibi davranıyor.

**4. İki `[Obsolete]` özellik silindi.** Hiçbir resource ve test kullanmıyordu; `System.Text.Json` eşleşmeyen anahtarı yok saydığı için 1.x locale dosyaları hâlâ parse ediliyor.

**5. `LocalizationModel.Currency` silindi, `WordifyOptions` constructor'ı eklendi.** Artık varsayılan para birimini adlandırmanın tek yolu var; validator'daki karşılıklı dışlama kuralı ve çözüm yolundaki bir dal ortadan kalktı. Convenience constructor para birimini `Currencies`'e `DefaultCurrencyKey` altında yazıyor (bunu doğrulayan test var). `CreateConverter` silindi — 3×3 dispatch matrisi üç yerde değil, bir yerde.

README ve CHANGELOG buna göre güncellendi; ayrıca kalite geçişinin yakaladığı yanlış README iddiası ("dual/paucal için custom localization yeter") düzeltildi — özel localization bunu çözmüyor, sebebi de yazıldı.

İstediğin noktadayız — tek engel bir kimlik bilgisi.

## Birleştirildi

PR #3 merge commit'iyle indi: `1651b69`, master'da. Öncesinde 7 check'in 7'si yeşildi (ubuntu + windows build/test, CodeQL csharp + actions, Snyk, submit-nuget). Branch'i silmedim.

## Tag

`v2.0.0` master'a atıldı. Bir not: **annotated tag push edilemedi** — Entire remote helper'ı tag objesini commit sanıp reddetti:

```
! [remote rejected] v2.0.0 -> v2.0.0
  (parse 9136393...: not a commit: type=tag)
```

Lightweight tag ile geçti. Yayın hattı tag adına baktığı için işlevsel fark yok, ama Entire remote'u kullanıldığı sürece annotated tag'ler bu repoda çalışmayacak.

## Yayın: hat çalıştı, anahtar çalışmadı

Publish workflow tetiklendi ve **son adım hariç her şey geçti**:

| Adım | Sonuç |
|---|---|
| Derive package version from tag | ✅ `PKG_VERSION=2.0.0` |
| Restore / Build | ✅ |
| Test | ✅ |
| Pack | ✅ |
| Verify the package carries the tagged version | ✅ `NumWordify.2.0.0.nupkg` |
| **Push to NuGet** | ❌ **403** |

```
error: Response status code does not indicate success: 403
(The specified API key is invalid, has expired, or does not have permission
 to access the specified package.)
```

Yani geçen turda düzeltilen şeylerin hepsi doğrulandı — sürüm gerçekten tag'den geliyor, paket dosya adı gerçekten kontrol ediliyor, `--skip-duplicate` olmadığı için hata yutulmuyor. Eskiden bu adım sessizce yeşil dönüyordu; şimdi dürüstçe kırmızı.

Sahiplik sorunu değil: nuget.org'da `NumWordify 1.0.0` yayında ve sahibi `keparlak`. Dolayısıyla `NUGET_API_KEY` ya süresi dolmuş (NuGet anahtarları en fazla 365 gün yaşar, 1.0.0 bir yıl önce yayınlanmış) ya da kapsamı `NumWordify`'ı içermiyor.

**Senin yapman gereken iki adım:**

1. nuget.org → API Keys → yeni anahtar; scope **Push → Push new package version**, paket olarak `NumWordify` (ya da glob `NumWordify*`). Sonra GitHub'da repo → Settings → Environments → `nuget` → `NUGET_API_KEY` secret'ını güncelle.
2. Bana haber ver, başarısız job'ı yeniden çalıştırayım:
   ```
   gh run rerun 31622941287 --failed -R keparlak/NumWordify
   ```

Hiçbir şey push edilmediği için yeniden çalıştırma temiz — yarım kalmış bir yayın yok. Anahtarı kendim üretemem ve secret'a dokunamam, o yüzden orada duruyorum.

Kalan işler yayını engellemiyor, hepsi merge sonrasına bıraktıklarımız: `global.json` → `latestMinor`, net48 için `Microsoft.NETFramework.ReferenceAssemblies`, CI'da net6.0/net7.0 testleri, `SupportedCultures`'ı `ReadOnlyCollection` ile sarma, `decimalPlaces` ↔ `scales.Length` doğrulaması. Bir de workflow'lar `actions/checkout@v5` / `setup-dotnet@v5` yükseltmesini istiyor — Node 20 deprecation uyarısı bu çalıştırmada da düştü.

Bulundu. Secret repo seviyesinde ve **süresi dolmuş**:

```
NUGET_API_KEY   2025-01-20T04:03:30Z
```

NuGet API anahtarları en fazla 365 gün yaşar. Bu anahtar 20 Ocak 2025'te oluşturulmuş, yani Ocak 2026 civarında ölmüş — bugün Ağustos 2026. 403'ün sebebi tam olarak bu. `nuget` environment'ının secret'ı olmadığı için GitHub repo seviyesindekine düşüyor; log'da `***` görünmesinin sebebi de o (var ama geçersiz).

## Yapılacaklar

**1. nuget.org'da yeni anahtar** — [nuget.org/account/apikeys](https://www.nuget.org/account/apikeys) → Create:
- Key Name: `numwordify-publish`
- Expires in: 365 gün
- Scopes: **Push → Push new package version**
- Select packages: `NumWordify` (ya da glob `NumWordify*`)

**2. Anahtarı `nuget` environment'ına koy** — az önceki ekranda **Add environment secret**, adı tam olarak `NUGET_API_KEY`. Repo seviyesindekini de sil (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions), böylece tek kaynak kalır. Environment secret'ı repo secret'ını zaten ezer, ama iki yerde tutmak bir sonraki sefer hangisinin geçerli olduğunu bulmayı zorlaştırır.

Workflow'daki yorum da bunu söylüyordu:

```yaml
# Requires an environment named "nuget" holding NUGET_API_KEY, so publishing can be
# gated on a reviewer rather than on whoever can push a tag.
environment: nuget

Based on the search results, here's the announcement information:

## NuGet.org API Key Expiration Announcement

Starting August 17, 2026, new API keys will be limited to 30 days, and all existing API keys created before that date will expire on November 1, 2026.

NuGet API key durations will be reduced to 30 days starting August 17th to significantly strengthen the integrity of the NuGet supply chain.

A 365-day duration will no longer be available for new API keys.

### Rationale
A NuGet.org API key is effectively a password for publishing packages, and when a long-lived key is stored in a repository secret, copied between systems, or embedded in a build configuration, a disclosure can give an attacker an extended opportunity to publish unauthorized package versions.

### Recommendations
The NuGet team strongly recommends moving to NuGet Trusted Publishing. Trusted Publishing is a modern publishing workflow that allows a CI/CD workflow to authenticate to NuGet.org through OpenID Connect (OIDC), with NuGet.org validating a signed, short-lived identity token and issuing a temporary API key for that publishing operation.

content.text:
Araştırma sonucu: **API key üretme, doğrudan Trusted Publishing'e geç.** Bu bir stil tercihi değil, takvimli bir zorunluluk.

## Neden

nuget.org'un [.NET Blog duyurusu](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/strengthening-nuget-supply-chain-security-reducing-api-key-lifetime/):

- **17 Ağustos 2026**'dan itibaren yeni API anahtarları **30 günle** sınırlı — 365 gün seçeneği kalkıyor. Bu beş gün sonra.
- O tarihten önce oluşturulmuş **her anahtar 1 Kasım 2026'da ölüyor.**

Yani şimdi anahtar üretsen: 30 günde bir aynı 403'ü yaşarsın. UI'daki "Not recommended" etiketi de bunun için.

[Trusted Publishing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/nuget-org/trusted-publishing) yerine geçen mekanizma: workflow GitHub'dan imzalı kısa ömürlü bir OIDC token istiyor, nuget.org onu senin tanımladığın policy'ye karşı doğrulayıp **1 saat geçerli** geçici bir anahtar veriyor. Repoda kalıcı hiçbir kimlik bilgisi durmuyor. Token bir kez kullanılabiliyor, o yüzden anahtar push'tan hemen önce isteniyor.

## Yaptığım değişiklik — PR #4

https://github.com/keparlak/NumWordify/pull/4

```yaml
    environment: nuget
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write        # GitHub'dan imzalı OIDC token istemek için

      - name: NuGet login
        uses: NuGet/login@v1
        id: login
        with:
          user: keparlak

      - name: Push to NuGet
        run: |
          dotnet nuget push "out/NumWordify.${PKG_VERSION}.nupkg" \
            --api-key "${{ steps.login.outputs.NUGET_API_KEY }}" \
            --source https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json
```

Hattın geri kalanı aynı: sürüm tag'den türüyor, üretilen dosya adı doğrulanıyor, `--skip-duplicate` hâlâ kasten yok.

Bir yan kazanç: `environment: nuget` policy'de de belirtildiği için, o environment dışında koşan bir run anahtar **alamıyor**. Reviewer kapısı ilk kez gerçek bir kapı oluyor — şu ana kadar dekoratifti.

## Senin yapman gereken tek şey

nuget.org → profil menüsü → **Trusted Publishing** → Create:

| Alan | Değer |
| --- | --- |
| Repository Owner | `keparlak` |
| Repository | `NumWordify` |
| Workflow File | `publish.yml` |
| Environment | `nuget` |

Sadece dosya adı — `.github/workflows/` yolunu yazma. Repo public olduğu için policy kalıcı olarak aktif başlamalı; private repolarda görülen "7 gün içinde bir yayın yapılmazsa pasifleşir" durumu bizde beklenmiyor.

Eski repo secret'ı `NUGET_API_KEY`'i de silebilirsin, artık hiçbir şey okumuyor.

## Sonra ben ne yapacağım

Bir ayrıntı var: `v2.0.0` tag'i `1651b69`'u gösteriyor ve o commit'te **eski** workflow var. Başarısız job'ı yeniden çalıştırmak eski dosyayı koşturur. Dolayısıyla sıra şu olacak:

1. PR #4'ün check'leri yeşillenince merge (şu an koşuyor).
2. `v2.0.0` tag'ini silip yeni master commit'ine yeniden atmak. Hiçbir şey yayınlanmadığı için 2.0.0'ı harcamaya gerek yok — sürüm numarası temiz.
3. Publish workflow'unu izlemek.

Policy'yi oluşturduğunda haber ver, üçünü de ben hallederim.
Policy'i oluşturdum.

content.text: Push başarılı — hem `.nupkg` hem `.snupkg` için `Created` + "Your package was pushed". nuget.org indeksleme doğrulaması sürüyor; tekrar bakıyorum:

**NumWordify 2.0.0 yayında.**

```
versions = ["1.0.0", "2.0.0"]
nupkg indirilebilir: HTTP 200, 193 KB
```

https://www.nuget.org/packages/NumWordify/2.0.0

Arama indeksi hâlâ `1.0.0` gösteriyor — o ayrı bir kuyruk, genelde birkaç dakika içinde yetişiyor. Paketin kendisi `dotnet add package NumWordify --version 2.0.0` ile şu an çekilebilir durumda.

## Bu turda olan biten

**Kod.** Üçüncü thermos turu çekirdekte kusur bulmadı — bağımsız yazılmış referans implementasyona karşı 508.040 değerde 0 uyuşmazlık. Bulunanlar çevredeydi ve hepsi kapatıldı: bozuk kültür koruması ve onu "doğrulayan" ama hiçbir ortamda kırılamayan test, tek başına test edilmemiş dört dilbilgisi bayrağı, iki ölü `[Obsolete]` özellik, `Currency`/`DefaultCurrency` ikiliği, üç yerde tekrarlanan dispatch matrisi. 277 → 296 test, üç hedefte de yeşil.

**Kural motoru.** Ölçümle reddedildi: algoritma ~200 satır, hiçbir metot 51 satırı ve hiçbir yer 4 iç içelik derinliğini aşmıyor, ve istenen kural zinciri deseni `TensAndOnesWord`'de zaten var. Gerçek kısıt şema ifade gücü — Rusça sondasında 10 vakadan 5'i başarısız oldu ve hepsi iki eksik kavrama indi: çoğul kategorisi ve ölçek sözcüğüyle cinsiyet uyumu. Beşinci dil geldiğinde bunları eklemek doğru hamle; ikisi de ~60 satır ve birincisi mevcut üç özel durumu siliyor.

**Yayın hattı.** 403'ün sebebi Ocak 2025'te üretilmiş ve süresi dolmuş bir anahtardı. Yeni anahtar üretmek işe yaramazdı: nuget.org 17 Ağustos'tan itibaren yeni anahtarları 30 günle sınırlıyor ve mevcut tüm anahtarları 1 Kasım'da öldürüyor. Trusted Publishing'e geçildi — repoda artık kalıcı hiçbir yayın kimlik bilgisi yok, workflow her seferinde 1 saatlik geçici anahtar alıyor. `NUGET_API_KEY` repo secret'ını artık silebilirsin, hiçbir şey okumuyor.

Kalan küçük borçlar duruyor: `global.json` → `latestMinor`, net48 için referans assembly paketi, CI'da net6.0/net7.0 testleri, `SupportedCultures`'ı `ReadOnlyCollection` ile sarma, `decimalPlaces` ↔ `scales.Length` doğrulaması, ve `actions/checkout@v5` + `setup-dotnet@v5` yükseltmesi — Node 20 deprecation uyarısı bu çalıştırmada da düştü. Hiçbiri acil değil; istersen bir sonraki oturumda 2.0.1 olarak toplarız.
önerinle devam edelim

Ultracode açık. Kalan borçları 2.0.1 olarak toplayacağım — önce her maddeyi bağımsız doğrulatıp kesin yama planı çıkarmak için bir workflow başlatıyorum, sonra uygulamayı ben yapıp ikinci turda çekişmeli inceleme koşturacağım.

export const meta = {
  name: 'numwordify-201-investigation',
  description: 'Verify and design each remaining post-2.0.0 cleanup for NumWordify, then reconcile the plans',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Investigate', detail: 'one read-only agent per cleanup item' },
    { title: 'Reconcile', detail: 'conflicts, ordering and missed interactions across all plans' },
  ],
}

const CONTEXT = `
Repo: C:\\Users\\empad\\Desktop\\Development\\entire\\numwordify — NumWordify, a .NET library
converting numbers to words across locales. Multi-target: netstandard2.0, net6.0, net7.0,
net8.0, net9.0. Branch: master at commit 632ea96. Version 2.0.0 was published to nuget.org
minutes ago; this work is for a 2.0.1 patch release, so PATCH-SAFE changes only — no
public API breaks.

Test project: tests/NumWordify.Tests (296 tests, currently targets net9.0, net8.0, and
net48 on Windows only). Build enforces analyzers and TreatWarningsAsErrors via
Directory.Build.props.

Note: \`gh\` cannot auto-detect the remote (it is an \`entire://\` remote), so pass
\`-R keparlak/NumWordify\` explicitly to any gh command.

RULES:
- Do NOT modify, create, or delete any file in the repository. This is investigation only.
- You MAY run \`dotnet build\`, \`dotnet test\`, and write throwaway probe code under the
  system temp directory to prove or disprove a claim.
- Prove your claim by reproducing it. "The code looks like it would" is not evidence.
  If you cannot reproduce it, say so and set stillPresent to false.
- Do not manufacture work. If the item turns out not to be a real problem, say SKIP and
  explain why — that is a valuable answer, not a failure.
`

const PLAN_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    item: { type: 'string', description: 'Short name of the item investigated' },
    verdict: { type: 'string', enum: ['DO', 'SKIP', 'NEEDS_DECISION'] },
    stillPresent: { type: 'boolean', description: 'Whether the defect/gap actually exists on master today, as reproduced by you' },
    evidence: { type: 'string', description: 'What you actually ran or observed. Include command output or probe results.' },
    edits: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          file: { type: 'string' },
          change: { type: 'string', description: 'What changes in this file and why' },
        },
        required: ['file', 'change'],
      },
    },
    exactPatch: { type: 'string', description: 'The precise before/after text for each edit, copy-pasteable. Quote the existing lines verbatim so they can be matched exactly.' },
    risks: { type: 'string', description: 'What could break, what interacts with other parts of the codebase, what you are unsure about' },
    tests: { type: 'string', description: 'The specific test(s) that should accompany this change, and what they assert. State if a test is not warranted and why.' },
    breaking: { type: 'boolean', description: 'True if this changes public API or observable behaviour in a way that is not patch-safe' },
  },
  required: ['item', 'verdict', 'stillPresent', 'evidence', 'edits', 'exactPatch', 'risks', 'tests', 'breaking'],
}

const ITEMS = [
  {
    key: 'global-json',
    task: `ITEM: global.json pins the .NET 9 SDK band and blocks contributors.

global.json contains "version": "9.0.100" with "rollForward": "latestFeature". A prior
review reproduced that latestFeature never crosses major.minor (asking for 8.0.100 with
latestFeature resolved to 8.0.424, not the installed 9.0.314; asking 11.0.100 failed with
"A compatible .NET SDK was not found"). So a contributor with only a .NET 10 SDK installed
cannot run dotnet restore or build at all. There was no global.json before this release.

Verify that claim yourself with throwaway global.json files in a temp directory. Then
determine the right setting. The stated justification for pinning was "a new SDK band
cannot turn a release build red without a code change" — check whether that is already
served by AnalysisLevel in Directory.Build.props (read it), in which case rollForward
latestMinor or latestMajor would keep the analyzer pin while unblocking newer SDKs.
Consider what each rollForward value would mean for the CI and publish workflows, which
install specific SDK versions via actions/setup-dotnet. Also check whether the README's
Contributing section mentions the SDK requirement.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'test-tfms',
    task: `ITEM: two shipped target frameworks are compiled but never tested.

The library targets netstandard2.0, net6.0, net7.0, net8.0 and net9.0. The test project
(tests/NumWordify.Tests/NumWordify.Tests.csproj) targets only net9.0, net8.0 and — on
Windows — net48. So net6.0 and net7.0 are built but no test ever runs against them.
The net48 leg does exercise the netstandard2.0 build.

Determine: should the test project add net6.0 and net7.0? Check whether those runtimes are
actually available on the GitHub Actions runners used by .github/workflows/ci.yml (read
it — note which SDKs setup-dotnet installs, and whether installing an SDK also provides
the matching runtime for test execution). Check whether xunit and the other test packages
referenced still support net6.0/net7.0. Note that net6.0 and net7.0 are both out of
support from Microsoft — weigh whether testing them is worth it versus dropping them from
the library's TargetFrameworks entirely (that second option is NOT patch-safe, so if you
think it is right, say so and mark it breaking).

SECOND, SEPARATE CONCERN in the same file: the test project adds net48 on Windows but has
no PackageReference to Microsoft.NETFramework.ReferenceAssemblies. It builds on this
machine and on windows-latest only because the 4.x targeting packs happen to be installed
by Visual Studio / Build Tools. A Windows contributor with only the .NET SDK would hit
MSB3644. Verify this reasoning against the csproj and confirm the exact package reference
and version that fixes it.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'supported-cultures-mutable',
    task: `ITEM: the process-wide cached culture list is handed out mutably.

Converters/LocalizationLoader.cs builds SupportedCultureNames as a Lazy<IReadOnlyList<string>>
whose value is a string[]. NumberToWordsConverter.SupportedCultures exposes it, and
LocalizationNotFoundException.AvailableCultures (Exceptions/NumWordifyException.cs) receives
it. A prior review reproduced that a caller can cast IReadOnlyList<string> back to string[]
and permanently corrupt the process-wide list, including the text of every future exception
message.

Reproduce that yourself against the built DLL. Then design the fix. Consider: wrapping in
ReadOnlyCollection<string>, returning a copy, or changing the field type. Weigh allocation
cost (SupportedCultures is on no hot path, but confirm that by finding its call sites).
Check whether LocalizationNotFoundException.AvailableCultures has the same problem
independently and whether it needs its own fix. Confirm ReadOnlyCollection<T> is available
on netstandard2.0. Note the loader's own doc comment claims "The cached instances are never
handed out to callers, which is what makes sharing them safe" — decide whether the comment
or the code is wrong, and say which.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'loader-case-sensitivity',
    task: `ITEM: a mixed-case embedded resource filename would break SupportedCultures.

Converters/LocalizationLoader.cs: ResourceNames filters manifest names with
EndsWith(".json", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase), but Load rebuilds the cache key as
CultureNameOf(name) + ResourceSuffix where ResourceSuffix is the lowercase ".json", and
GetManifestResourceStream is case-sensitive. A future Resources/de-DE.JSON would therefore
make SupportedCultures throw InvalidLocalizationException for every caller.

All five shipped files are lowercase, so this is latent. Verify the mechanism precisely by
reading the code and, if you can, by constructing a probe (you may create a throwaway
project in the system temp directory that embeds a mixed-case .JSON resource and links the
loader source, or reason from an exact reading if a probe is impractical — say which you
did). Then decide whether this deserves a fix at all: a latent bug reachable only by a
future maintainer adding a mis-cased file could equally be handled by a test that asserts
every embedded resource name is lowercase, which is cheaper and fails at the right moment.
Recommend the option you would defend, not the one that touches the most code.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'decimal-places-validation',
    task: `ITEM: the validator does not cross-check decimalPlaces against scales.Length.

Converters/LocalizationValidator.cs validates settings.decimalPlaces is 0..6 but never
compares it with numbers.scales.Length. The fractional part is rendered through
ConvertWholeNumber (Converters/NumberToWordsConverter.cs), so decimalPlaces > 3 needs a
thousands scale word. A prior review reported that a locale with scales: [""] and
decimalPlaces: 6 passes validation, then Convert(1.123456m) throws
NumberOutOfRangeException with a message blaming the whole part:
"The number 1,123456 is too large for this locale: it defines 1 scale word(s), so the
largest convertible value is 10^3 - 1." — when the whole part is just 1.

Reproduce this. Then work out the exact rule: for a given decimalPlaces, what is the
minimum scales.Length required so that the fraction can always be rendered? Derive it from
the code, do not guess — consider the largest possible fraction value for N decimal places
and how ConvertWholeNumber groups it. Verify your rule holds at every boundary from
decimalPlaces 0 through 6 with probe locales. Confirm no shipped locale in Resources/*.json
would be rejected by the new rule. Draft the validator error message in the voice of the
existing ones (read several first — they state the problem and the fix).`,
  },
  {
    key: 'exception-culture-leak',
    task: `ITEM: an exception message formats a decimal with the current culture.

Exceptions/NumWordifyException.cs: NumberOutOfRangeException interpolates the offending
value into its message, which uses CurrentCulture, so a Turkish machine reports
"The number 1,123456 is too large" where every other number-to-string in the output path
correctly uses InvariantCulture.

Confirm it, then AUDIT THE WHOLE LIBRARY for the same class of mistake — every string
interpolation, ToString, string.Format, string.Join and Convert of a number, decimal, int
or enum in any user-visible message or in any code path that produces output. Report every
site you find, not just this one. For each, say whether it is a real problem or benign and
why. Also check the reverse direction: any parsing or comparison that should be culture
invariant but is not (string comparisons, ToUpper/ToLower without a culture argument,
etc.). Note that analyzers are enabled with TreatWarningsAsErrors — explain why CA1305 /
CA1307 style rules did not already catch these, since that tells us whether the analyzer
configuration itself should change (check Directory.Build.props and .editorconfig).`,
  },
  {
    key: 'actions-v5',
    task: `ITEM: workflow actions target deprecated Node 20.

Both .github/workflows/ci.yml and .github/workflows/publish.yml use actions/checkout@v4 and
actions/setup-dotnet@v4, which target Node 20. Every run now emits: "Node.js 20 is
deprecated. The following actions target Node.js 20 but are being forced to run on Node.js
24."

Research the CURRENT state (today is August 2026) using web search and by fetching the
release notes / README of actions/checkout and actions/setup-dotnet: what is the latest
major version of each, does it run on Node 24, and are there any breaking changes between
v4 and the latest that would affect these two workflows? Read both workflow files and say
exactly what changes. Also check whether NuGet/login@v1 (used in publish.yml) has the same
Node deprecation issue, and whether github/codeql-action and any other action referenced
anywhere under .github/ needs the same bump — list every action reference in the repo and
its status. Be precise about version pinning style: report what the repo currently uses
(tag vs SHA) and whether to keep it.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'converter-internal-cleanup',
    task: `ITEM: two behaviour-preserving cleanups inside the converter.

Read Converters/NumberToWordsConverter.cs fully first.

(a) SIX null-forgiving suppressions. \`_localization.Numbers!\` appears at roughly lines 312,
327, 370, 401, 472 and 499, each usually preceded by \`var numbers = _localization.Numbers!;\`.
The invariant is real — after LocalizationValidator.Validate, Numbers is never null — but
the type still says NumbersModel?, so every consumer re-asserts it. Proposed fix: capture
\`private readonly NumbersModel _numbers;\` and \`private readonly SettingsModel _settings;\`
once in the single private constructor where validation has just run, then read those
fields everywhere. Check this carefully against two things: the documented contract that a
caller-supplied LocalizationModel "must not be mutated after it has been given to a
converter", and the Pow10 guard which deliberately re-reads a property at call time to
catch a mutated decimalPlaces. Determine whether caching the field objects weakens any
existing guard or test. Find every test that depends on post-construction mutation of a
model (grep the test project) and report them.

(b) "What follows this group" is derived three different ways: ConvertWholeNumber computes
scaleIsNoun/followedByNoun (~line 341), HundredsWord computes endsNumeralPhrase (~line 407),
and OverrideBeforeFollowingWord computes beforeNumeralAdjective/beforeNoun (~line 446).
KindOf(scale) is called from three separate sites, and ConvertWholeNumber has an
\`out bool endsWithNounScale\` that one of its two call sites discards as \`out _\`.
Proposed fix: a private enum Following { Nothing, NumeralAdjective, Noun } computed once and
threaded through, with ConvertWholeNumber returning a tuple instead of using an out param.

For (b), you must PROVE the proposed mapping is exactly equivalent, not merely plausible.
Enumerate the truth table of (scale, KindOf(scale), currencyFollows) and show the current
expressions and the proposed ones agree in every row, including scale == 0 with and without
a currency. If any row disagrees, that is the finding — report it and stop recommending the
refactor as-is.

Both are patch-safe internal changes. Say clearly whether each is worth doing in a patch
release or should wait, and why.`,
  },
]

phase('Investigate')

const plans = await parallel(ITEMS.map(it => () => agent(
  `${CONTEXT}\n\n${it.task}`,
  { label: `investigate:${it.key}`, phase: 'Investigate', schema: PLAN_SCHEMA, effort: 'high' },
)))

const good = plans.filter(Boolean)
log(`${good.length}/${ITEMS.length} investigations returned`)

phase('Reconcile')

const RECON_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    conflicts: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          files: { type: 'string' },
          description: { type: 'string' },
          resolution: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['files', 'description', 'resolution'],
      },
    },
    applyOrder: {
      type: 'array',
      items: { type: 'string' },
      description: 'Item keys in the order they should be applied, with grouping notes',
    },
    dropped: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' }, description: 'Items that should NOT be done, with the reason' },
    missed: { type: 'string', description: 'Anything the eight investigations collectively failed to consider' },
    releaseAdvice: { type: 'string', description: 'Whether this is a legitimate 2.0.1 patch, and what the release notes should say' },
  },
  required: ['conflicts', 'applyOrder', 'dropped', 'missed', 'releaseAdvice'],
}

const recon = await agent(
  `${CONTEXT}

Eight independent investigations of proposed NumWordify 2.0.1 cleanups have completed.
Here are their structured results:

${JSON.stringify(good, null, 2)}

Your job is to reconcile them, and to be sceptical of them.

1. CONFLICTS: find every case where two plans touch the same file or the same lines, or
   where one plan's edit would invalidate another's exactPatch. Say how to resolve each.
2. APPLY ORDER: give the order the edits should be applied in, grouping edits to the same
   file together so a later edit never has to re-anchor on text an earlier one changed.
3. DROP: which items should not be done at all? Be willing to cut. A patch release that
   changes less is a better patch release. Anything marked breaking:true must be dropped
   from 2.0.1 — say so explicitly and note it for a later minor/major.
4. MISSED: read the repository yourself. What did all eight investigations collectively
   fail to consider? Look especially for: interactions between their proposed changes,
   anything in the diff between v1.0.0 and v2.0.0 that is still unaddressed, and whether
   any proposed change is actually observable to a consumer (which would make it not
   patch-safe).
5. RELEASE ADVICE: is this a legitimate 2.0.1, and what should the CHANGELOG say?

Verify claims rather than trusting them. If an investigation's evidence does not actually
support its verdict, say so — that is the most valuable thing you can report.`,
  { label: 'reconcile', phase: 'Reconcile', schema: RECON_SCHEMA, effort: 'high' },
)

return { plans: good, reconciliation: recon }

2.0.0 yayında, master temiz ve origin ile senkron. 2.0.1 için sekiz maddeyi paralel olarak bağımsız ajanlara doğrulattırıyorum — her biri kusuru **yeniden üretmeden** plan yazmayacak, sonra dokuzuncu bir ajan planları uzlaştırıp çakışmaları ve kesilmesi gerekenleri çıkaracak.

İncelenen maddeler:

Uzlaştırıcıya ayrıca şunu söyledim: kesmeye istekli ol, ve `breaking: true` işaretlenen her şey 2.0.1'den düşsün. Sonuçlar gelince uygulamayı ben yapıp ikinci turda çekişmeli inceleme koşturacağım.

Casting the declared `IReadOnlyList<string>` back to `string[]` and writing to it rewrote the supported-culture listing and the text of every subsequent \"localization not found\" message for the life of the process. Both now return a genuinely read-only collection.\n\n### Changed\n\n- `NumberToWordsConverter.SupportedCultures` and `LocalizationNotFoundException.AvailableCultures` still declare `IReadOnlyList<string>`, but their runtime type is now `ReadOnlyCollection<string>` rather than `string[]`. Code that cast the result to `string[]` compiled against 2.0.0 and will now throw `InvalidCastException`. That cast was never supported and was the defect above, but the change is silent to the compiler, so it is called out here.\n- The build now validates the public API against the published 2.0.0 package, so an accidental break fails the build rather than reaching a consumer.\n\nAnd say plainly what is NOT in it, so the next release has a record: the decimalPlaces-vs-scales validation rule and the LocalizationLoader simplification are held for 2.1.0; the NumberToWordsConverter refactor is held pending a fix for the ScaleKind divergence found during review; the SDK pin, workflow action bumps and net6.0/net7.0 test coverage land on master unreleased."

TESTS:
Warranted — this class of bug is invisible to a suite that never leaves the developer's culture, and right now no test in tests/NumWordify.Tests ever sets CurrentCulture (grep: every CultureInfo reference is InvariantCulture used for parsing test data). That is exactly why it shipped.

Add one file, tests/NumWordify.Tests/InvariantMessageTests.cs, with three tests. Pick cultures that break in different ways so the test cannot pass by accident: tr-TR (comma separator), sv-SE (U+2212 negative sign), ar-SA (U+066B separator, U+061C-prefixed negative).

1. Out-of-range message, positive:
   [Theory] InlineData("tr-TR"), ("sv-SE"), ("ar-SA"), ("de-DE")
   Set CultureInfo.CurrentCulture in a try/finally that restores it. Assert.Throws<NumberOutOfRangeException>(() => 1000000000000000000.5m.ToWords("en-US")), then
   Assert.Contains("The number 1000000000000000000.5 is too large", ex.Message, StringComparison.Ordinal).
   Asserts the literal invariant rendering, so it fails on master under every one of those cultures (verified: tr-TR yields "...,5", ar-SA yields "...٫5").

2. Out-of-range message, negative — this is the one that catches the NegativeSign half, which the positive case cannot:
   Same shape with -1000000000000000000.5m, asserting Assert.Contains("-1000000000000000000.5", ex.Message, StringComparison.Ordinal) with an ASCII hyphen. Fails on master under sv-SE (U+2212) and ar-SA (U+061C).

3. Validator message with a negative int:
   Under sv-SE, build a minimal-but-valid LocalizationModel with Settings.DecimalPlaces = -3 (ones/tens/hundreds arrays of 10 with index 0 = "" and the rest non-empty, Scales = [""], ZeroWord/NegativeWord set, CurrencyFormat/NumberFormat = "{whole}"), pass it to new NumberToWordsConverter(model), and assert the InvalidLocalizationException message Contains "but is -3." with an ASCII hyphen, StringComparison.Ordinal. Repeat with SpecialNumbers.Special = { [-5] = "x" } asserting "contains the key -5.". Both fail on master under sv-SE.

Mechanics that matter: restore CurrentCulture in finally, and put the class in its own xunit collection (or [Collection("Culture")]) so the ambient mutation cannot race the parallel suite — CurrentCulture is per-thread so it is already safe in practice, but the collection makes that explicit. Do not use CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentCulture, which leaks across the whole run. All three cultures resolve on net48 as well as net9.0/net8.0, so the file needs no TFM guard; assert only on the invariant text, never on what the hostile culture produces, so NLS-vs-ICU differences on net48 cannot make it flaky.

Also worth adding cheaply, since the audit proved it and nothing currently locks it in: a test that converts under CurrentCulture=tr-TR and ar-SA and asserts the conversion output equals the en-US-run output (e.g. 1234.56m.ToWords("en-US") == "ONE THOUSAND TWO HUNDRED THIRTY-FOUR DOLLARS FIFTY-SIX CENTS", plus one es-ES case exercising the int-keyed special map and one fr-FR case exercising the ScaleKind enum). That pins the JSON-parse and output paths as culture-independent, which is currently true only by luck of System.Text.Json's invariant behaviour.
